usage: Polite past; the everyday way to say you submitted an application

I applied to that company.
Mark the company with 에, not 를: 회사에 지원하다

지원하려고 하다 = 'be about to / planning to apply'

It is an honor to apply for the sales position at your company.

english: to have / take a job interview
usage: I have an interview / I'm interviewing
Polite; the everyday phrasing from the candidate's side
examples: 내일 면접 봐요.
I have an interview tomorrow.
From the candidate's side the verb is 보다 ('see/take'), not 하다
오후에 면접 보러 가는데 너무 떨려요.
I'm going to an interview this afternoon and I'm so nervous.
면접 보러 가다 = heading off to interview; 떨리다 = 'to be nervous'
1차 면접 봤는데 분위기 괜찮았어요.
I had the first-round interview and the vibe was okay.
1차 면접 = first-round; companies often run 2차, 3차 too
nuance: 면접 (Sino-Korean 面接, 'face + meet') is the job interview, and the verb that pairs with it from YOUR side as the candidate is 보다 — literally 'to see/take', the same 보다 you use for 시험 보다 ('take an exam'). This collocation is the single biggest pitfall for English speakers, who calque 'do an interview' into 면접 하다 — but 면접하다 sounds like the COMPANY is conducting/administering the interview, i.e. the interviewer's side, so a candidate saying 저 면접 해요 sounds off. Say 면접 봐요. The matching pair is 시험 보다 / 시험 치다 ('take a test'), so think of an interview as a test you 'take'. From the employer's angle they 면접을 진행하다 ('conduct the interview') or 면접관 ('interviewer') 이 면접을 보다 can also occur, but as a learner-candidate, lock in 면접 보다. usage: Polite past; 내다 ('to hand in') is the natural verb
Could you look over my résumé?
Polite request to have it reviewed
examples: 이력서 어디로 보내면 돼요?
Where should I send my résumé?
보내다 ('send') for email; 내다 ('submit') for handing in
이력서에 경력 사항을 더 자세히 적었어요.
I wrote my work history in more detail on my résumé.
경력 사항 = 'career/work-history details'; 적다 = 'to write down'
이력서랑 자기소개서 같이 첨부해서 메일로 보내 주세요.
Please attach both your résumé and cover letter and email them.
첨부하다 = 'to attach (a file)'
nuance: 이력서 (Sino-Korean 履歷書, 'career-record document') is your résumé/CV — the form listing your education and work history. The big content note for English speakers: a Korean 이력서 traditionally pairs with a separate 자기소개서 ('self-introduction document', the cover-letter-style essay, often shortened to 자소서), and many applications expect BOTH. Don't merge them — the 이력서 is the fact sheet (dates, titles), the 자기소개서 is the narrative ('why me'). A second culture point: traditional Korean 이력서 often included a photo, birth date, and personal details that Western résumés omit, though many modern/foreign companies have dropped the photo. usage: Polite; what the interviewer typically says to you
Formal; very common opening line from an interviewer
Polite, slightly encouraging; 한번 ... 보세요 = 'give it a try'
Adds 간단하게 ('briefly'), a frequent real instruction
examples: 먼저 자기소개 좀 해 주세요.
First, please introduce yourself.
먼저 ('first') signals this is the opening question
네, 자기소개 간단하게 부탁드릴게요.
Yes, a brief self-introduction, please.
부탁드릴게요 softens the request; common from a polite interviewer
그럼 1분 정도로 자기소개 한번 해 보시겠어요?
Then could you introduce yourself in about a minute?
1분 정도로 ('in about a minute') — interviewers often set a time
nuance: 자기소개 (Sino-Korean 自己紹介, 'self-introduction') is the opening ritual of nearly every Korean interview, and 자기소개 좀 해 주세요 is what the INTERVIEWER says to you — so you'll mostly HEAR this and need to respond, not say it yourself. The verb is 소개하다 ('to introduce'); note 자기소개하다 can be one word, or you split it as 자기소개(를) 해 주세요. The 좀 here is the politeness softener (not 'a little bit of'), and 해 주세요 frames it as a courteous request. English speakers make two errors. First, they answer by literally translating 'My name is...' and stop — but a Korean 자기소개 is expected to be a short pitch: name, background, the role you're applying for, a strength, and 잘 부탁드립니다 to close; just stating your name feels incomplete. Second, when they themselves want to introduce someone else, they reuse 자기소개 — but 자기소개 is reflexive ('introduce ONESELF'); to introduce another person it's just 소개하다 (제 친구를 소개할게요). Saying 자기소개를 만들어 주세요.

english: I look forward to working with you / Please consider me favorably
usage: I look forward to it; please treat me well
Formal-humble; the standard closing of a self-introduction
I will be in your care / please consider me well
Polite but softer, for peers or a casual setting
I look forward to working with you going forward
Adds 앞으로 ('from now on'), said once hired or starting
examples: 이상입니다. 잘 부탁드립니다.
That's all. I look forward to it; thank you for your consideration.
이상입니다 ('that concludes it') + 잘 부탁드립니다 closes your self-intro
꼭 함께 일하고 싶습니다. 잘 부탁드리겠습니다.
I really want to work with you. Please consider me favorably.
Strengthened with -겠습니다 at the end of an interview
오늘부터 출근합니다. 앞으로 잘 부탁드립니다.
I start today. I look forward to working with you all.
Said on your first day to new colleagues
nuance: 잘 부탁드립니다 is one of the most important and untranslatable Korean phrases: 잘 ('well') + 부탁 ('a request/favor') + 드리다 (humble 'to give', so 'I humbly make a request'). It has no clean English equivalent — depending on context it means 'please treat me well', 'I look forward to working with you', 'please consider my application favorably', or 'thanks in advance for your help'. In an interview it closes your 자기소개 and your final remarks, signaling humility and goodwill. The humble verb 드리다 (not the plain 하다) is what makes it interview-appropriate; 잘 부탁해요 is the softer peer version and 잘 부탁드리겠습니다 is the most deferential. The English-speaker error is twofold: first, trying to translate it literally and producing something like '저를 잘 다뤄 주세요' ('please handle me well') — which sounds bizarre; you must use the set phrase. Second, omitting it entirely because English interviews don't have a parallel — but skipping 잘 부탁드립니다 makes a Korean self-introduction feel abrupt and a little arrogant. Note it can also mean 'please do this for me' in office life (이거 잘 부탁드립니다 = 'please take good care of this task'), so context decides whether it's a greeting or a request. Always pair it with a slight bow in person.

What is your motivation for applying?

Was there something that led you to apply?
계기 ('trigger/occasion') — asks for the spark behind it

솔직히 지원 동기가 궁금해서요. 왜 이 직무를 택하셨어요?

직무 = 'job role/duties'; 택하다 = 'to choose'

usage: Polite past; the standard happy announcement
Formal; for an announcement or to a superior

Casual everyday synonym; 붙다 lit. 'to stick'

english: I didn't get it / I was rejected

Polite; the neutral, formal way to say it

Softer, face-saving; 안 되다 = 'it didn't happen'

이번엔 ('this time') frames it as one attempt, not the end

nuance: 이상입니다 literally is 이상 (以上, 'the above / that much') + 입니다 ('it is'), i.e. 'that is the extent of it' — the crisp, formal way to signal you've FINISHED speaking, used to cap a 자기소개, an interview answer, or a presentation. It tells the listener 'I'm done, your turn', which matters in interviews because trailing off ambiguously leaves the interviewer unsure whether to jump in. English speakers underuse this because English has no exact single-word equivalent (you'd just stop talking), and the result is awkward dead air; learning to land on 이상입니다 or 여기까지입니다 makes you sound composed and structured. Two pitfalls: (1) the homonym confusion — 이상 also shows up in 이상하다 ('to be weird/abnormal') and as 'more than' (3개 이상 = 'three or more'); but as a standalone closing 이상입니다 it purely means 'that's all'. Don't let 이상하다 ('to be strange') bleed into it. (2) The 직역 trap: translating 'that's all' as 그게 다예요 is fine in casual speech but too light for a formal interview close; 이상입니다 carries the right businesslike register. For an even more formal sign-off (end of a longer talk) use 이상으로 마치겠습니다 ('with that, I will conclude'). Register: 이상입니다 is formal-polite and exactly right for interviews; the casual equivalent among peers would be 이게 다야 (반말). Always follow it with 감사합니다 and a slight bow.
